title: Implication and biconditional columns
brief: Fill the missing entries of a four-row truth table, then state the rule behind each column.
hint: An implication fails in exactly one row. A biconditional is true when the two values match.
code:
p  q |  p → q    p ↔ q
T  T |  {{1}}      T
T  F |  {{2}}      F
F  T |  {{3}}      F
F  F |  T        {{4}}

Rules behind the columns
  p → q is false only when p is {{5}} and q is false.
  p ↔ q is true exactly when the two values {{6}}.

blanks.explanation: p is true and q is true, so the promise p → q holds. Type the capital letter T.
This is the single row that breaks an implication: a true hypothesis with a false conclusion.
With p false the implication is vacuously true, whatever q says.
Both values are false here, so they agree and the biconditional is true.
The implication only fails when the hypothesis is true and the conclusion is false.
p ↔ q is the claim that the two sides carry the same truth value.

steps: Rows 1 and 4 carry matching values, so the biconditional is true in both, and row 1 also makes the implication true.
Row 2 (p = T, q = F) is the one false row of p → q, and row 3 (p = F, q = T) is vacuously true because a false hypothesis promises nothing.
This gap-filling sheet is matched against the authored answers, so type T and F exactly as the table shows them; nothing here is executed.

title: Translating English into connectives
brief: Choose the connective or formula that matches each English sentence, with p and q fixed at the top.
hint: "q if p" puts p first. "q only if p" puts p last.
code:
Let  p = "the switch is on"   and   q = "the lamp lights".

a) The lamp lights if the switch is on.
       p {{1}} q

b) The lamp lights only if the switch is on.
       q {{2}} p

c) It is not the case that both are true.
       ¬ ( p {{3}} q )

d) The switch is off but the lamp still lights.
       {{4}} ∧ q

e) The lamp lights exactly when the switch is on.
       {{5}}

f) The converse of "if p then q" is
       {{6}}

blanks.explanation: "if the switch is on" is the hypothesis, so the sentence is p → q.
"only if" introduces the necessary condition, which sits in the consequent: q → p.
"both are true" is the conjunction p ∧ q, and the sentence denies it.
"but" behaves like ∧ while asserting the switch is off, so the left literal is ¬p.
"exactly when" binds in both directions, which is the biconditional.
The converse swaps hypothesis and conclusion; ¬q → ¬p is the contrapositive and ¬p → ¬q is the inverse.

steps: Sentences a and b describe the same pair of facts in different directions: a is p → q, b is q → p.
Negation applies to whichever connective joins the two statements inside it, so c needs ∧ before the ¬ and d needs ¬p before the ∧.
Only e and f ask for a whole formula: "exactly when" is ↔, and the converse is the swap, not the negation.

title: Reading both normal forms off a table
brief: Turn the eight rows of a three-variable function into the clauses and minterms that build its normal forms.
hint: A clause comes from a false row: disjoin the literals, negating every variable that is true in that row.

blanks.explanation: Row (T, T, F) makes x, y and ¬z true, so the clause that is false exactly there uses ¬x, ¬y and z.
Row (F, T, T): x is false so it appears plain, while the true y and z appear negated.
Row (F, T, F): only y is true, so only y is negated in this clause.
A minterm for row (F, F, F) conjoins the negation of each variable, and all three are false in that row.
Each CNF clause is false on exactly one row, so the clauses are collected from the false rows.
Each minterm is true on exactly one row, so the DNF lists the true rows.

steps: The three false rows produce the full CNF (¬x ∨ ¬y ∨ z) ∧ (x ∨ ¬y ∨ ¬z) ∧ (x ∨ ¬y ∨ z), which is the answer to the matching mock-exam question.
The five true rows produce the full DNF with five minterms; a shorter DNF is still a DNF but not a full one.
Check any clause by substituting its own row: the false row makes every literal false, so that clause and the whole CNF fail, while every other row satisfies it.

title: Full CNF and full DNF of one proposition
brief: Work both normal forms of [(p → q) ∧ q] → p from its truth table and name the shape of each.
hint: One false row gives one CNF clause; the other three rows give the three minterms of the DNF.
code:
F = [(p → q) ∧ q] → p

p  q |  F
T  T |  T
T  F |  T
F  T |  {{1}}
F  F |  T

CNF(F) = {{2}}                 one clause, from the single false row
DNF(F) = (p ∧ q) ∨ {{3}} ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q)

A normal form is called {{4}} when every variable appears in every bracket.
A CNF joins its clauses with {{5}}, and each clause is a disjunction of {{6}}.
The DNF above has {{7}} minterms, one for each true row.

blanks.explanation: At p = F, q = T both p → q and q are true, so the hypothesis holds while the conclusion p fails.
The false row is p = F, q = T, so the clause negates each of those values: p from ¬p, and ¬q from q being true.
The second true row is p = T, q = F, whose minterm is p ∧ ¬q.
A full (canonical) normal form mentions every variable in every bracket, which is what the truth-table recipe guarantees.
Conjunctive normal form is a conjunction of disjunctions, so ∧ sits between the clauses.
A literal is a variable or its negation; a clause disjoins literals.
Three rows are true, so the full DNF has three minterms.

steps: Evaluate the hypothesis (p → q) ∧ q first: it is true only at (T, T) and (F, T), and in the second of those the conclusion p is false.
CNF reads the false rows and DNF reads the true rows, which is why this proposition has a one-clause CNF and a three-term DNF.
The typed gap in the last line expects the plain digit 3, matching the three true rows of the table.

title: Choosing the quantifier and the connective
brief: Match each English statement to the right quantifier and the right connective inside it.
hint: The golden rules: ∀ travels with →, and ∃ travels with ∧.
code:
Domain: all students in the class.
P(x) = "x passes the test",   D(x) = "x takes discrete mathematics".

a) Every student takes discrete mathematics.
       {{1}}x D(x)

b) At least one student takes discrete mathematics.
       {{2}}x D(x)

c) Nobody takes discrete mathematics.
       ∀x {{3}} D(x)

d) Everything that passes the test takes the course.
       ∀x ( P(x) {{4}} D(x) )

e) Something both passes the test and takes the course.
       ∃x ( P(x) {{5}} D(x) )

f) The domain of discourse is
       {{6}}

blanks.explanation: "every" quantifies over the whole domain.
"at least one" is an existence claim.
"nobody takes it" says every student fails to take it, so the predicate is negated inside a universal.
A universal restriction uses the universal conditional; with ∧ it would claim every student both passes and takes the course.
An existence claim needs both properties true of the same object; with → the statement would be satisfied by anything that does not pass.

options: the set of objects the variables range over
the set of connectives the language allows
blanks.answer: the set of objects the variables range over
blanks.explanation: The domain fixes what x may stand for, which decides the truth of every quantified statement.

steps: Pair the quantifier with the connective that matches the shape of the claim: universal claims restrict with →, existential claims witness with ∧.
A negated universal, ∀x ¬D(x), is the same statement as "nobody takes the course", while ¬∃x D(x) is its equivalent through the negation rules.
Swap the pairs in d and e and both statements change meaning, which is why the pairing is worth memorising.

title: Translating about cars, then negating nested quantifiers
brief: Finish three translations over the domain of cars, then push negations past one and two quantifiers.
hint: Each negation that crosses a quantifier flips it: ∀ becomes ∃ and ∃ becomes ∀.
code:
Domain: all cars.
S(x) = "x is a sports car",  F(x) = "x is fast",  E(x) = "x is expensive".

a) All sports cars are fast.
       ∀x ( S(x) {{1}} F(x) )

b) There are fast cars that are not sports cars.
       ∃x ( F(x) {{2}} ¬S(x) )

c) Every fast sports car is expensive.
       ∀x ( ( S(x) {{3}} F(x) ) → E(x) )

Negation rules
       ¬∀x P(x)   ≡   {{4}}x ¬P(x)
       ¬∃x P(x)   ≡   {{5}}x ¬P(x)
       ¬∀x ∀y P(x, y)   ≡   {{6}}x {{7}}y ¬P(x, y)

blanks.explanation: A universal conditional: take any car, and if it is a sports car then it is fast.
The existential claims one car that is fast and is not a sports car at the same time.
Both properties belong in the hypothesis, so they conjoin inside the antecedent while the outer connective stays →.
"Not everything has P" means something lacks P.
"Nothing has P" means every object lacks P.
The outer ∀ flips first when the negation crosses it.
Every quantifier the negation passes is flipped, so both become ∃ and only the predicate keeps the ¬.

steps: Statements a to c are the three tutorial translations: universal with →, existential with ∧, and a two-part hypothesis conjoined inside the antecedent.
For the nested case, move the negation one quantifier at a time: ¬∀x ∀y P becomes ∃x ¬∀y P, then ∃x ∃y ¬P.
Order matters once quantifiers differ: ∃y ∀x is not equivalent to ∀x ∃y, so a swapped pair is not a legal simplification.

title: The three steps on a sum formula
brief: Fill the arithmetic that carries the classic proof of 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1) / 2 from P(1) to P(k + 1).
hint: The inductive step only ever adds the next term to both sides of the hypothesis, then tidies the algebra.
code:
Prove  1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1) / 2  for every positive integer n.

1. Basis step.     Substitute {{1}} and check that both sides equal 1.
2. Hypothesis.     Assume the sum of the first k integers is {{2}}.
3. Inductive step. The term that must be added to both sides is {{3}}.
4. Factor.         k(k + 1) / 2 + (k + 1) = (k + 1)(k + 2) / {{4}},
                   which is the closed form taken at {{5}}.
5. Conclude.       The statement holds for every positive integer by {{6}}.

blanks.explanation: The claim starts at the first positive integer, so the basis step substitutes n = 1 and gets 1 = 1.
The inductive hypothesis is P(k): the closed form with k in place of n. Write it exactly as authored; spacing between k and the bracket is ignored but the divisor 2 is not.
P(k) stops at k, so P(k + 1) has one extra term, namely k + 1.
Factoring (k + 1) out of k(k + 1)/2 + (k + 1) leaves ((k + 1)(k + 2))/2, so the divisor stays 2.
The expression just derived is the closed form evaluated at n = k + 1, which is exactly P(k + 1).
A true basis step plus a valid step from P(k) to P(k + 1) is the principle of mathematical induction.

steps: The basis step anchors the chain; the hypothesis names P(k) without claiming it for every n.
Adding k + 1 to both sides and putting the right side over the common divisor 2 gives (k + 1)(k + 2) / 2, the closed form at k + 1.
Typed gaps are compared with the authored solution after spacing is normalised, so equivalent rewrites such as (k + 1)*k/2 are not recognised even though a mathematician would accept them.

title: A divisibility proof, term by term
brief: Complete the rewrite that proves 7^n − 2^n is a multiple of 5 for every non-negative integer n.
hint: Pull a 7 out of 7^(k+1) so the hypothesis expression appears, then repair the coefficient of 2^k.
code:
Prove that 7^n − 2^n is divisible by 5 for every non-negative integer n.

Basis.        n = 0 gives 7^0 − 2^0 = {{1}}, and 5 divides that value.
Hypothesis.   Assume 7^k − 2^k = 5m for some integer m.
Inductive step. Rewrite the next difference as

      7^(k+1) − 2^(k+1)  =  {{2}} ( 7^k − 2^k )  +  {{3}} * 2^k

The first summand is a multiple of 5 because of {{4}}; the second is 5
times an integer.  Spot check the next case: 7^1 − 2^1 = {{5}}, and the
claim is stated for every n ≥ {{6}}.

blanks.explanation: 7^0 − 2^0 = 1 − 1 = 0, and every integer divides 0, so the basis step holds.
Taking 7 out of 7^(k+1) gives 7(7^k − 2^k), which is where the hypothesis can be used.
7(7^k − 2^k) subtracts 7·2^k, but only 2·2^k should be subtracted, so 5·2^k must be added back.
7^k − 2^k = 5m is exactly the assumption, so 7 times it is 35m.
7 − 2 = 5, which is divisible by 5, confirming the case n = 1.
The statement covers non-negative integers, so the chain begins at n = 0 rather than n = 1.

steps: Expanding the completed line gives 7^(k+1) − 7·2^k + 5·2^k = 7^(k+1) − 2·2^k = 7^(k+1) − 2^(k+1), so the rewrite really is the next power difference.
Both summands carry a factor of 5, which is the whole argument: the first through the hypothesis, the second by inspection.
The same shape appears in the tutorial item 3 divides 2^(2n) − 1: rewrite the next power so the hypothesis expression reappears, then show the leftover term is divisible as well.
